title: Ἄνεμοι καὶ σῆμα
titleEn: The Winds and the Mound — Iliad 23.192–286
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: The pyre of Patroclus will not catch, so Achilles stands apart and prays to the North Wind and the West Wind, pouring wine from a golden cup and promising fine sacrifices. Iris carries the prayer to the winds, who are feasting at the house of the West Wind; she will not sit, since she is going back to the Ethiopians’ sacrifice, and they rush over the sea to Troy and fall on the pyre. Achilles pours wine and mourns all night. At dawn the fire dies down and the winds go home. Achilles sleeps until the leaders gather, then tells them to quench the pyre with wine, gather the bones into a golden bowl in a double layer of fat, and raise only a modest mound. They do so, and Achilles seats the people and brings out prizes for the chariot race. He says he would take the first prize himself, but his immortal horses are standing in grief for Patroclus, and he calls on anyone who trusts his horses and chariot to enter.

sentences.t: οὐδὲ πυρὴ Πατρόκλου ἐκαίετο τεθνηῶτος·
sentences.tr: oude pyrē Patroklou ekaieto tethnēōtos·
sentences.l: And the pyre of dead Patroclus was not burning;
sentences.i: Yet the pyre of the dead Patroclus was not burning;
sentences.n: The part begins with a pyre that will not take light. οὐδέ is ‘and not’ and ἐκαίετο the imperfect of καίω ‘burn’, here intransitive: ‘was not burning’. Πατρόκλου is the genitive of Πάτροκλος, the dead man; τεθνηῶτος is the genitive singular of the perfect participle of θνῄσκω ‘die’ (‘dead’), with the epic ending -ηῶτ- for Attic -εῶτ-. Achilles set the pyre alight in the previous part (23.177), and the next lines say why it does not burn.

sentences.t: ἔνθ’ αὖτ’ ἀλλ’ ἐνόησε ποδάρκης δῖος Ἀχιλλεύς·
sentences.tr: enth’ aut’ all’ enoēse podarkēs dios Achilleus·
sentences.l: Then in turn another thing devised swift-footed, heavenly Achilles:
sentences.i: Then swift-footed, heavenly Achilles thought of something else:
sentences.n: ἔνθ’ αὖτ’ is ‘then, in turn’. The edition prints ἀλλ’ here with no accent mark, which would normally be ἀλλά ‘but’; the same words at 23.140 are printed ἄλλ’ ‘another thing’, and the sense here is the same, so the line is read as ἄλλ’ ἐνόησε ‘thought of another thing’. ἐνόησε is the aorist of νοέω ‘think of, devise’. ποδάρκης δῖος Ἀχιλλεύς is the stock epithet pair ‘swift-footed, heavenly Achilles’. The colon leads to his prayer.

sentences.t:
στὰς ἀπάνευθε πυρῆς δοιοῖς ἠρᾶτ’ ἀνέμοισι
Βορέῃ καὶ Ζεφύρῳ, καὶ ὑπίσχετο ἱερὰ καλά·
sentences.tr:
stas apaneuthe pyrēs doiois ērat’ anemoisi
Boreēi kai Zephyrōi, kai hypischeto hiera kala·
sentences.l:
standing apart from the pyre, he prayed to two winds,
to the North Wind and the West Wind, and promised fine sacrifices;
sentences.i: He stood apart from the pyre and prayed to two winds, the North Wind and the West Wind, and promised fine sacrifices;
sentences.n: στάς is the aorist participle of ἵστημι ‘stand’, and ἀπάνευθε πυρῆς ‘apart from the pyre’ takes the genitive. ἠρᾶτ’ is the imperfect of ἀράομαι ‘pray’, ὑπίσχετο the imperfect of ὑπισχνέομαι ‘promise’. δοιοῖς is ‘two’ (Attic δυοῖν). Βορέῃ and Ζεφύρῳ are datives, the winds named as figures. ἱερὰ καλά ‘fine sacrifices’ is formulaic. Line 195 is metrically irregular as transmitted, at its opening: the first foot scans only if the short first syllable of Βορέῃ is lengthened and its -εῃ is read as one syllable (synizesis).

sentences.t:
πολλὰ δὲ καὶ σπένδων χρυσέῳ δέπαϊ λιτάνευεν
ἐλθέμεν, ὄφρα τάχιστα πυρὶ φλεγεθοίατο νεκροί,
sentences.tr:
polla de kai spendōn chryseōi depaï litaneuen
elthemen, ophra tachista pyri phlegethoiato nekroi,
sentences.l:
and much also, pouring a libation with a golden cup, he entreated them
to come, so that as quickly as possible with fire the dead might blaze,
sentences.i: and, pouring libations from a golden cup, he entreated them at length to come, so that the dead might blaze up in the fire as quickly as possible,
sentences.n: σπένδων is the present participle of σπένδω ‘pour a libation’, with χρυσέῳ δέπαϊ ‘a golden cup’ (epic dative in -αϊ). πολλά is adverbial, ‘much, at length’. λιτάνευεν is the imperfect of λιτανεύω ‘entreat’, and ἐλθέμεν the epic infinitive of ἔρχομαι (= ἐλθεῖν). ὄφρα with the optative φλεγεθοίατο (epic -οίατο for -οιντο, from φλεγέθω ‘blaze’) gives the aim. νεκροί are ‘the dead’: Patroclus and the victims laid on the pyre.

sentences.t: ὕλη τε σεύαιτο καήμεναι.
sentences.tr: hylē te seuaito kaēmenai.
sentences.l: and the wood might rush to burn.
sentences.i: and the wood might hurry to burn.
sentences.n: This still belongs to the ὄφρα clause of the previous unit. ὕλη is the wood heaped for the pyre. σεύαιτο is the optative of σεύω ‘set in rapid motion’, which in the middle means ‘rush, hurry’, and καήμεναι is the epic infinitive of καίω (= καῆναι), ‘to burn’, passive in sense and giving the result the wood is to hurry towards. τε joins this to the previous wish.

sentences.t:
ὦκα δὲ Ἶρις
ἀράων ἀΐουσα μετάγγελος ἦλθ’ ἀνέμοισιν.
sentences.tr:
ōka de Iris
araōn aïousa metangelos ēlth’ anemoisin.
sentences.l:
and quickly Iris,
hearing the prayers, went as go-between messenger to the winds.
sentences.i: And Iris, hearing the prayers, went quickly to the winds as a go-between messenger.
sentences.n: ὦκα is ‘quickly’ and goes with ἦλθ’. Ἶρις is the gods’ messenger. ἀΐουσα is the present participle of ἀΐω ‘hear’, which takes the genitive ἀράων: ἀρή is ‘prayer’, with the epic genitive plural -άων. μετάγγελος is a compound of μετά ‘between, among’ and ἄγγελος ‘messenger’: she goes between Achilles and the winds. ἦλθ’ is the aorist of ἔρχομαι, and ἀνέμοισιν the dative ‘to the winds’.

sentences.t:
οἳ μὲν ἄρα Ζεφύροιο δυσαέος ἀθρόοι ἔνδον
εἰλαπίνην δαίνυντο·
sentences.tr:
hoi men ara Zephyroio dysaeos athrooi endon
eilapinēn dainynto·
sentences.l:
They indeed then, of the ill-blowing West Wind, all together within
a banquet were feasting;
sentences.i: They, for their part, were all together inside at the ill-blowing West Wind’s, feasting at a banquet;
sentences.n: οἳ μέν is the article-form as a pronoun, ‘they’, the winds Iris is looking for. Ζεφύροιο δυσαέος is ‘of the ill-blowing West Wind’ (δυσαής: δυσ- ‘bad’ + ἄημι ‘blow’), and ἔνδον ‘within’ stands without a noun: they are in his house. ἀθρόοι is ‘all together, in a crowd’. εἰλαπίνην is the accusative of εἰλαπίνη ‘banquet’, and δαίνυντο the imperfect middle of δαίνυμι ‘feast’.

sentences.t:
θέουσα δὲ Ἶρις ἐπέστη
βηλῷ ἔπι λιθέῳ·
sentences.tr:
theousa de Iris epestē
bēlōi epi litheōi·
sentences.l:
and running, Iris stood by
at the threshold of stone;
sentences.i: and Iris, running, came and stood at the stone threshold;
sentences.n: θέουσα is the present participle of θέω ‘run’, and ἐπέστη the aorist of ἐφίστημι ‘stand at, stand by’. βηλῷ ἔπι is ἐπὶ βηλῷ with the accent thrown back (anastrophe); βηλός is the threshold, and λιθέῳ ‘of stone’ is the adjective of λίθος. The unit begins in the middle of line 201.

sentences.t:
τοὶ δ’ ὡς ἴδον ὀφθαλμοῖσι
πάντες ἀνήϊξαν, κάλεόν τέ μιν εἰς ἓ ἕκαστος·
sentences.tr:
toi d’ hōs idon ophthalmoisi
pantes anēïxan, kaleon te min eis he hekastos·
sentences.l:
and they, when they saw her with their eyes,
all sprang up, and each called her to himself;
sentences.i: and when they saw her with their own eyes, they all sprang up, and each of them called her to himself;
sentences.n: τοί is the article-form as a pronoun, ‘they’, the winds. ὡς ἴδον is ‘when they saw’ (ἴδον is the aorist of ὁράω, without augment). ἀνήϊξαν is the aorist of ἀναΐσσω ‘spring up’. κάλεον is the imperfect of καλέω, unaugmented, and μιν the epic enclitic ‘her’. εἰς ἓ is ‘to himself’, each wind wanting her at his own side; ἕκαστος ‘each one’ is the subject in apposition to πάντες.

sentences.t: ἣ δ’ αὖθ’ ἕζεσθαι μὲν ἀνήνατο, εἶπε δὲ μῦθον·
sentences.tr: hē d’ auth’ hezesthai men anēnato, eipe de mython·
sentences.l: but she in turn rejected sitting down, and spoke a word:
sentences.i: But she rejected the invitation to sit down, and spoke a word:
sentences.n: ἣ δ’ αὖθ’ is ‘but she in turn’, αὖθ’ being αὖτε. ἕζεσθαι is the infinitive of ἕζομαι ‘sit’, and ἀνήνατο the aorist of ἀναίνομαι ‘reject’; what she rejects is the winds’ call to sit, so the English says ‘invitation’. εἶπε δὲ μῦθον ‘and spoke a word’ closes the line and opens Iris’ speech, which runs to 211.

sentences.t:
οὐχ ἕδος· εἶμι γὰρ αὖτις ἐπ’ Ὠκεανοῖο ῥέεθρα
Αἰθιόπων ἐς γαῖαν,
sentences.tr:
ouch hedos· eimi gar autis ep’ Ōkeanoio rheethra
Aithiopōn es gaian,
sentences.l:
“No sitting; for I am going back again to the streams of Oceanus,
to the land of the Ethiopians,
sentences.i: “There is no sitting for me; for I am going back to the streams of Oceanus, to the land of the Ethiopians,
sentences.n: οὐχ ἕδος has no verb: ἕδος is ‘seat, sitting’, so ‘there is no sitting’, a polite refusal. εἶμι is the present of εἶμι ‘go’, with future sense, and αὖτις ‘back again’. Ὠκεανοῖο is the epic genitive of Ὠκεανός, the great river round the world, and ῥέεθρα the neuter plural ‘streams’. ἐπ’ and ἐς both mean ‘to’. Αἰθιόπων is the genitive plural, ‘of the Ethiopians’.

sentences.t:
ὅθι ῥέζουσ’ ἑκατόμβας
ἀθανάτοις, ἵνα δὴ καὶ ἐγὼ μεταδαίσομαι ἱρῶν.
sentences.tr:
hothi rhezous’ hekatombas
athanatois, hina dē kai egō metadaisomai hirōn.
sentences.l:
where they are sacrificing hecatombs
to the immortals, so that I too may share in the offerings.
sentences.i: where they are sacrificing hecatombs to the immortals, so that I too may share in the offerings.
sentences.n: ὅθι is ‘where’. ῥέζουσ’ is ῥέζουσι, the present 3rd plural of ῥέζω ‘do’, which with ἑκατόμβας means ‘sacrifice hecatombs’. ἀθανάτοις is the dative ‘to the immortals’. μεταδαίσομαι is from μεταδαίομαι ‘share in a feast’, taking the genitive ἱρῶν (ἱρά = ἱερά, ‘sacrifices, offerings’); the form can be a future or a short-vowel subjunctive after ἵνα.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ Ἀχιλεὺς Βορέην ἠδὲ Ζέφυρον κελαδεινὸν
ἐλθεῖν ἀρᾶται, καὶ ὑπίσχεται ἱερὰ καλά,
sentences.tr:
all’ Achileus Boreēn ēde Zephyron keladeinon
elthein aratai, kai hypischetai hiera kala,
sentences.l:
But Achilles prays that the North Wind and the resounding West Wind
come, and promises fine sacrifices,
sentences.i: But Achilles is praying that the North Wind and the resounding West Wind may come, and promising fine sacrifices,
sentences.n: Iris repeats Achilles’ prayer back to the winds. Βορέην and Ζέφυρον are accusatives, the subject of the infinitive ἐλθεῖν after ἀρᾶται ‘prays’ (accusative and infinitive). κελαδεινόν is ‘resounding’, from κέλαδος ‘din’. ὑπίσχεται ‘promises’ is the present of ὑπισχνέομαι. Ἀχιλεύς has a single λ for the metre.

sentences.t:
ὄφρα πυρὴν ὄρσητε καήμεναι, ᾗ ἔνι κεῖται
Πάτροκλος, τὸν πάντες ἀναστενάχουσιν Ἀχαιοί.
sentences.tr:
ophra pyrēn orsēte kaēmenai, hēi eni keitai
Patroklos, ton pantes anastenachousin Achaioi.
sentences.l:
so that you may rouse the pyre to burn, in which lies
Patroclus, for whom all the Achaeans groan aloud.”
sentences.i: so that you may rouse the pyre to burn, the pyre on which Patroclus lies, whom all the Achaeans mourn with groans.”
sentences.n: ὄφρα with the aorist subjunctive ὄρσητε (from ὄρνυμι ‘rouse’) gives the purpose; καήμεναι is the epic infinitive ‘to burn’. ᾗ ἔνι is ἐν ᾗ with the accent thrown back, ‘in which’, the relative referring to πυρήν. κεῖται is ‘lies’. τόν is the relative ‘whom’, and ἀναστενάχουσιν the present of ἀναστενάχω ‘groan over, lament’. Iris’ speech ends here.

sentences.t: ἣ μὲν ἄρ’ ὣς εἰποῦσ’ ἀπεβήσετο,
sentences.tr: hē men ar’ hōs eipous’ apebēseto,
sentences.l: She indeed then, so having spoken, went away,
sentences.i: So she spoke and went away,
sentences.n: ἣ μὲν ἄρ’ ὣς εἰποῦσ’ ἀπεβήσετο ‘So she spoke and went away’ is the formula for a speaker’s exit, here with the aorist middle ἀπεβήσετο of ἀποβαίνω (the same form at 2.35). εἰποῦσ’ is the aorist participle ‘having spoken’. The line begins a paragraph in the edition.

sentences.t:
τοὶ δ’ ὀρέοντο
ἠχῇ θεσπεσίῃ νέφεα κλονέοντε πάροιθεν.
sentences.tr:
toi d’ oreonto
ēchēi thespesiēi nephea kloneonte paroithen.
sentences.l:
and they hurried off
with a wondrous din, throwing the clouds into confusion before them.
sentences.i: and the two winds hurried off with a wondrous din, throwing the clouds into confusion before them.
sentences.n: τοί is the winds, now two, and the dual participle κλονέοντε (from κλονέω ‘throw into confusion’) agrees with them as a pair. ὀρέοντο is an epic form with the root of ὄρνυμι ‘rouse’, imperfect in force: ‘hurried off’, as at 2.398. ἠχῇ θεσπεσίῃ is ‘with a wondrous din’, a dative of manner. νέφεα is the epic uncontracted ‘clouds’, and πάροιθεν ‘before them, in front’.

sentences.t:
αἶψα δὲ πόντον ἵκανον ἀήμεναι, ὦρτο δὲ κῦμα
πνοιῇ ὕπο λιγυρῇ·
sentences.tr:
aipsa de ponton hikanon aēmenai, ōrto de kyma
pnoiēi hypo ligyrēi·
sentences.l:
And quickly the open-sea they reached to blow, and the wave rose
beneath the clear-sounding blast;
sentences.i: Quickly they came to the open sea, blowing, and the wave rose under the clear-sounding blast;
sentences.n: αἶψα ‘quickly’. ἵκανον is the imperfect of ἱκάνω ‘come to’, with the accusative πόντον ‘open sea’, and ἀήμεναι is the epic infinitive of ἄημι ‘blow’, giving the purpose or manner of their coming. ὦρτο is the aorist middle of ὄρνυμι ‘rose’. πνοιῇ ὕπο is ὑπὸ πνοιῇ, with the accent thrown back, ‘beneath the blast’; λιγυρῇ is ‘clear-sounding’.

sentences.t: Τροίην δ’ ἐρίβωλον ἱκέσθην,
sentences.tr: Troiēn d’ eribōlon hikesthēn,
sentences.l: and rich-clodded Troy the two reached,
sentences.i: and the two reached rich-soiled Troy,
sentences.n: Τροίην is the accusative of Τροίη, the epic form of Troy’s name. ἐρίβωλον ‘rich-clodded’ is the stock adjective for good farmland, here used of the Trojan land. ἱκέσθην is the dual of the aorist of ἱκνέομαι ‘come to’: the two winds, Boreas and Zephyrus, arrive together.

sentences.t: ἐν δὲ πυρῇ πεσέτην, μέγα δ’ ἴαχε θεσπιδαὲς πῦρ.
sentences.tr: en de pyrēi pesetēn, mega d’ iache thespidaes pyr.
sentences.l: and on the pyre they two fell, and loudly roared the wondrous-blazing fire.
sentences.i: and fell upon the pyre, and the wondrous-blazing fire roared aloud.
sentences.n: ἐν … πεσέτην is split by tmesis from ἐμπίπτω ‘fall upon’, and πεσέτην is the dual aorist of πίπτω. ἴαχε is the aorist of ἰάχω ‘cry out, roar’, and μέγα the adverb ‘loudly’. θεσπιδαὲς πῦρ is the formula for fire that blazes wondrously (θέσπις ‘divine’ + δαίω ‘burn’), here the pyre catching at last.

sentences.t:
παννύχιοι δ’ ἄρα τοί γε πυρῆς ἄμυδις φλόγ’ ἔβαλλον
φυσῶντες λιγέως·
sentences.tr:
pannychioi d’ ara toi ge pyrēs amydis phlog’ eballon
physōntes ligeōs·
sentences.l:
And all night long they, together, were hurling the flame of the pyre,
blowing clearly;
sentences.i: All night long the two, together, kept tossing the pyre’s flame, blowing with a clear sound;
sentences.n: παννύχιοι ‘all night long’ is an adjective agreeing with τοί γε, the winds. ἄμυδις is ‘together’. ἔβαλλον is the imperfect of βάλλω ‘throw’, so ‘kept throwing’ the flame. φυσῶντες is the present participle of φυσάω ‘blow’, and λιγέως the adverb of λιγύς ‘clear-sounding’.

sentences.t:
ὃ δὲ πάννυχος ὠκὺς Ἀχιλλεὺς
χρυσέου ἐκ κρητῆρος ἑλὼν δέπας ἀμφικύπελλον
οἶνον ἀφυσσόμενος χαμάδις χέε,
sentences.tr:
ho de pannychos ōkys Achilleus
chryseou ek krētēros helōn depas amphikypellon
oinon aphyssomenos chamadis chee,
sentences.l:
And he, all night long, swift Achilles,
having taken a double cup from a golden mixing-bowl,
drawing wine, poured it on the ground,
sentences.i: while swift Achilles, all night long, took a double cup from a golden mixing-bowl and, drawing wine, poured it out on the ground,
sentences.n: ὃ δέ ‘but he’ turns from the winds to Achilles. πάννυχος is ‘all night long’, and ὠκύς ‘swift’. ἑλών is the aorist participle of αἱρέω ‘take’, taking δέπας ἀμφικύπελλον, the ‘double cup’ (its exact shape is disputed) out of the κρητήρ, the bowl in which wine is mixed. ἀφυσσόμενος ‘drawing’ is from ἀφύσσω. χαμάδις is ‘to the ground’, and χέε the unaugmented imperfect of χέω ‘pour’.

sentences.t:
δεῦε δὲ γαῖαν
ψυχὴν κικλήσκων Πατροκλῆος δειλοῖο.
sentences.tr:
deue de gaian
psychēn kiklēskōn Patroklēos deiloio.
sentences.l:
and wetted the earth,
calling on the soul of miserable Patroclus.
sentences.i: and wet the earth, calling on the soul of miserable Patroclus.
sentences.n: δεῦε is the unaugmented imperfect of δεύω ‘wet’, and γαῖαν ‘earth’ the object. κικλήσκων is the present participle of κικλήσκω ‘call’, and ψυχήν ‘soul’ is what he calls, so that the dead man’s spirit may come to the offering. Πατροκλῆος is the epic genitive of Πατροκλῆς (Attic Πάτροκλος), and δειλοῖο the epic genitive of δειλός ‘miserable’.

sentences.t:
ὡς δὲ πατὴρ οὗ παιδὸς ὀδύρεται ὀστέα καίων
νυμφίου, ὅς τε θανὼν δειλοὺς ἀκάχησε τοκῆας,
sentences.tr:
hōs de patēr hou paidos odyretai ostea kaiōn
nymphiou, hos te thanōn deilous akachēse tokēas,
sentences.l:
And as a father laments for the bones of his own son, burning them,
a bridegroom, who by dying has grieved his miserable parents,
sentences.i: As a father mourns while burning the bones of his own son, a bridegroom whose death has grieved his miserable parents,
sentences.n: A simile opens with ὡς δέ ‘and as’; the matching ὣς in the next unit gives the application. οὗ is the possessive ‘his own’, and ὀδύρεται the present of ὀδύρομαι ‘lament’. ὀστέα ‘bones’ is the epic uncontracted form (Attic ὀστᾶ). νυμφίου is ‘bridegroom’, in apposition to παιδός. ὅς τε is a relative with generalising τε; θανών is the aorist participle ‘having died’, and ἀκάχησε the aorist of ἀκαχίζω ‘grieve’. δειλούς is ‘miserable’.

sentences.t:
ὣς Ἀχιλεὺς ἑτάροιο ὀδύρετο ὀστέα καίων,
ἑρπύζων παρὰ πυρκαϊὴν ἁδινὰ στεναχίζων.
sentences.tr:
hōs Achileus hetaroio odyreto ostea kaiōn,
herpyzōn para pyrkaïēn hadina stenachizōn.
sentences.l:
so Achilles lamented the bones of his companion, burning them,
creeping beside the pyre, groaning heavily.
sentences.i: so Achilles mourned as he burned the bones of his companion, crawling beside the pyre and groaning heavily.
sentences.n: ὣς … answers the ὡς δέ of the simile: Achilles is the father. ὀδύρετο is the imperfect of ὀδύρομαι ‘lament’. ἑτάροιο is the epic genitive of ἑταῖρος ‘companion’. ἑρπύζων is the present participle of ἑρπύζω ‘creep, crawl’. πυρκαϊήν is the pyre. ἁδινά, a neuter plural used as an adverb, is ‘heavily’ (ἁδινός ‘thick, crowded’), and στεναχίζων ‘groaning’ is from στεναχίζω.

sentences.t:
ἦμος δ’ ἑωσφόρος εἶσι φόως ἐρέων ἐπὶ γαῖαν,
ὅν τε μέτα κροκόπεπλος ὑπεὶρ ἅλα κίδναται ἠώς,
sentences.tr:
ēmos d’ heōsphoros eisi phoōs ereōn epi gaian,
hon te meta krokopeplos hypeir hala kidnatai ēōs,
sentences.l:
And at the time when the dawn-bringer goes to tell of light over the earth,
after which saffron-robed Dawn spreads herself over the sea,
sentences.i: And at the hour when the dawn-bringer comes to tell of light over the earth, and after it saffron-robed Dawn spreads herself over the sea,
sentences.n: ἦμος … τῆμος (in 228) is ‘at the time when … then’. ἑωσφόρος is ‘the dawn-bringer’, the morning star. εἶσι is the present of εἶμι ‘go, come’, and ἐρέων the future participle of ἐρέω ‘say, tell’, so ‘to tell of light’. ὅν τε μέτα is μετὰ ὅν ‘after which’, with the accent thrown back. κροκόπεπλος ‘saffron-robed’ is Dawn’s stock epithet. κίδναται ‘spreads herself’ is the present middle of κίδνημι, and ὑπεὶρ ἅλα ‘over the sea’.

sentences.t: τῆμος πυρκαϊὴ ἐμαραίνετο, παύσατο δὲ φλόξ.
sentences.tr: tēmos pyrkaïē emaraineto, pausato de phlox.
sentences.l: then the pyre was dying down, and the flame ceased.
sentences.i: then the pyre died down, and the flame ceased.
sentences.n: τῆμος answers ἦμος of the previous unit: ‘then’. πυρκαϊή is the pyre, and ἐμαραίνετο is the imperfect passive of μαραίνω ‘quench, die down’. παύσατο is the aorist middle of παύω, ‘ceased’, here with φλόξ ‘flame’ as its subject.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ἄνεμοι πάλιν αὖτις ἔβαν οἶκον δὲ νέεσθαι
Θρηΐκιον κατὰ πόντον·
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ anemoi palin autis eban oikon de neesthai
Thrēïkion kata ponton·
sentences.l:
And the winds back again went, to go home
over the Thracian open-sea;
sentences.i: And the winds went back again, to go home across the Thracian sea;
sentences.n: οἳ δ’ ἄνεμοι ‘and the winds’. ἔβαν is the epic aorist of βαίνω ‘go’, and πάλιν αὖτις ‘back again’. οἶκον δέ ‘homeward’ has the ending -δε of motion towards, and νέεσθαι is the infinitive of νέομαι ‘go home’, expressing purpose. Θρηΐκιον is ‘Thracian’; κατά with the accusative here means ‘over, across’. πόντον is the open sea.

sentences.t: ὃ δ’ ἔστενεν οἴδματι θύων.
sentences.tr: ho d’ estenen oidmati thyōn.
sentences.l: and it groaned, raging with a swell.
sentences.i: and the sea groaned, surging with a swell.
sentences.n: ὃ δ’ is ‘and it’, referring to πόντος ‘open sea’ in the previous unit. ἔστενεν is the imperfect of στένω ‘groan’. οἴδματι is the dative of οἶδμα ‘swell’, and θύων the present participle of θύω ‘rush, rage’, used of the sea churned by the winds as they leave.

sentences.t:
Πηλεΐδης δ’ ἀπὸ πυρκαϊῆς ἑτέρωσε λιασθεὶς
κλίνθη κεκμηώς,
sentences.tr:
Pēleïdēs d’ apo pyrkaïēs heterōse liastheis
klinthē kekmēōs,
sentences.l:
And Peleus’-son, from the pyre to one side having drawn away,
lay down, weary,
sentences.i: And the son of Peleus drew away from the pyre to one side and lay down, worn out,
sentences.n: Πηλεΐδης is a patronymic, ‘son of Peleus’, here Achilles. ἀπὸ … λιασθείς is ‘having drawn away from’, the aorist passive participle of λιάζομαι, and ἑτέρωσε ‘to one side’. κλίνθη is the aorist passive of κλίνω, ‘lay down’. κεκμηώς is the perfect participle of κάμνω ‘be weary’, in the epic form with -ηώς for Attic -ηκώς.

sentences.t: ἐπὶ δὲ γλυκὺς ὕπνος ὄρουσεν·
sentences.tr: epi de glykys hypnos orousen·
sentences.l: and upon him sweet sleep sprang;
sentences.i: and sweet sleep leapt upon him;
sentences.n: ἐπὶ … ὄρουσεν is split by tmesis from ἐπορούω ‘spring upon’, and ὄρουσεν is the aorist of ὀρούω ‘spring, rush’. γλυκὺς ὕπνος is ‘sweet sleep’, the sleep that comes on him after the night’s mourning. The colon after it leads to the noise that wakes him.

sentences.t: οἳ δ’ ἀμφ’ Ἀτρεΐωνα ἀολλέες ἠγερέθοντο·
sentences.tr: hoi d’ amph’ Atreïōna aollees ēgerethonto·
sentences.l: and they about Atreus’-son in a close mass were gathering;
sentences.i: and the others were gathering in a close mass about the son of Atreus;
sentences.n: οἳ δέ is ‘and they’, the Achaean leaders, in contrast with Achilles. Ἀτρεΐωνα is the accusative of Ἀτρεΐων, a patronymic equivalent to Ἀτρεΐδης, ‘son of Atreus’, here Agamemnon. ἀολλέες is ‘in a close mass’. ἠγερέθοντο is the imperfect middle of a verb meaning ‘gather’ (related to ἀγείρω).

sentences.t: τῶν μιν ἐπερχομένων ὅμαδος καὶ δοῦπος ἔγειρεν,
sentences.tr: tōn min eperchomenōn homados kai doupos egeiren,
sentences.l: of them coming up, the din and the thud woke him,
sentences.i: as they came up, the uproar and the thud woke him,
sentences.n: τῶν … ἐπερχομένων is a genitive absolute, ‘as they came up’, the present middle participle of ἐπέρχομαι. μιν is the epic enclitic ‘him’, Achilles. ὅμαδος καὶ δοῦπος is ‘the din and the thud’, the noise of many men and their feet. ἔγειρεν is the imperfect of ἐγείρω ‘wake’.

sentences.t: ἕζετο δ’ ὀρθωθεὶς καί σφεας πρὸς μῦθον ἔειπεν·
sentences.tr: hezeto d’ orthōtheis kai spheas pros mython eeipen·
sentences.l: and he sat, having raised himself upright, and spoke a word to them:
sentences.i: He sat up and spoke a word to them:
sentences.n: ἕζετο is the past tense of ἕζομαι ‘sit’, and ὀρθωθείς the aorist passive participle of ὀρθόω ‘set upright’, so ‘sat up’. σφεας is the epic accusative ‘them’. πρὸς μῦθον ἔειπεν is a formula, ‘spoke a word to’, with πρός split from the verb by tmesis (προσέειπεν). The colon introduces Achilles’ speech, which runs to 248.

sentences.t: Ἀτρεΐδη τε καὶ ἄλλοι ἀριστῆες Παναχαιῶν,
sentences.tr: Atreïdē te kai alloi aristēes Panachaiōn,
sentences.l: “Atreus’-son, and you other best men of the Achaeans all together,
sentences.i: “Son of Atreus, and you other best men of all the Achaeans,
sentences.n: Ἀτρεΐδη is the vocative, Agamemnon addressed first. ἀριστῆες ‘best men’ names the leaders, and Παναχαιῶν is the epic genitive of Παναχαιοί ‘the Achaeans all together’. This is a stock address to the whole body of chiefs, used elsewhere in the poem with the same English. The sentence continues in the next unit.

sentences.t:
πρῶτον μὲν κατὰ πυρκαϊὴν σβέσατ’ αἴθοπι οἴνῳ
πᾶσαν, ὁπόσσον ἐπέσχε πυρὸς μένος·
sentences.tr:
prōton men kata pyrkaïēn sbesat’ aithopi oinōi
pasan, hoposson epesche pyros menos·
sentences.l:
first with fire-faced wine quench the pyre throughout,
all of it, as far as the might of the fire reached;
sentences.i: first quench the whole pyre with wine that has the look of fire, as far as the might of the fire has reached;
sentences.n: σβέσατ’ is σβέσατε, the aorist imperative of σβέννυμι ‘quench’, with κατά split from it by tmesis (κατασβέσατε). πᾶσαν agrees with πυρκαϊήν ‘pyre’. αἴθοπι οἴνῳ is the stock ‘wine that has the look of fire’ (αἴθοψ). ὁπόσσον ἐπέσχε is ‘as far as … reached’, the aorist of ἐπέχω, and πυρὸς μένος ‘the might of the fire’ recalls 23.177.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα
ὀστέα Πατρόκλοιο Μενοιτιάδαο λέγωμεν
εὖ διαγιγνώσκοντες·
sentences.tr:
autar epeita
ostea Patrokloio Menoitiadao legōmen
eu diagignōskontes·
sentences.i: and then let us gather up the bones of Patroclus, son of Menoetius, taking care to tell them apart;
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα is ‘and then’. λέγωμεν is the hortative subjunctive of λέγω in its old sense ‘pick out, gather’, not ‘say’. Πατρόκλοιο is the epic genitive, and Μενοιτιάδαο a patronymic (‘son of Menoetius’) with the epic ending -άο. εὖ διαγιγνώσκοντες is ‘distinguishing well’, the present participle of διαγιγνώσκω ‘tell apart’. The unit begins in the middle of line 238.

sentences.t: ἀριφραδέα δὲ τέτυκται·
sentences.tr: ariphradea de tetyktai·
sentences.l: and they are very plain;
sentences.i: and they are very plain;
sentences.n: ἀριφραδέα is the neuter plural of ἀριφραδής ‘very plain’, easy to make out, agreeing with the bones just named. τέτυκται is the perfect passive of τεύχω, ‘has been made’, and with a neuter plural subject the verb is singular; here it simply means ‘is’. The reason follows with γάρ.

sentences.t:
ἐν μέσσῃ γὰρ ἔκειτο πυρῇ, τοὶ δ’ ἄλλοι ἄνευθεν
ἐσχατιῇ καίοντ’ ἐπιμὶξ ἵπποι τε καὶ ἄνδρες.
sentences.tr:
en messēi gar ekeito pyrēi, toi d’ alloi aneuthen
eschatiēi kaiont’ epimix hippoi te kai andres.
sentences.l:
for he lay in the middle of the pyre, and the others apart,
at the edge, were burning, in confusion, horses and men.
sentences.i: for he lay in the middle of the pyre, while the others, horses and men in confusion, burned apart from him at the edge.
sentences.n: ἔκειτο is the imperfect of κεῖμαι ‘lie’, with the dead Patroclus as subject. τοὶ δ’ ἄλλοι ‘and the others’ are the animals and men killed for the pyre; ἄνευθεν ‘apart’. ἐσχατιῇ is the dative ‘at the edge’. καίοντ’ is καίοντο, the imperfect passive of καίω, with its final vowel elided. ἐπιμίξ is ‘in confusion’, an adverb from μίγνυμι ‘mix’.

sentences.t:
καὶ τὰ μὲν ἐν χρυσέῃ φιάλῃ καὶ δίπλακι δημῷ
θείομεν, εἰς ὅ κεν αὐτὸς ἐγὼν Ἄϊδι κεύθωμαι.
sentences.tr:
kai ta men en chryseēi phialēi kai diplaki dēmōi
theiomen, eis ho ken autos egōn Aïdi keuthōmai.
sentences.l:
And these, indeed, in a golden bowl and double fat
let us put, until I myself am hidden in Hades.
sentences.i: And these let us put in a golden bowl, in a double layer of fat, until I myself am hidden in Hades.
sentences.n: τὰ μέν ‘these’ are the bones. φιάλη is a wide, shallow bowl. δίπλακι agrees with δημῷ ‘fat’ and means ‘double’, the bones wrapped in a double layer of fat. θείομεν is the epic aorist subjunctive of τίθημι, ‘let us put’. εἰς ὅ κεν with a subjunctive means ‘until’; κεύθωμαι is the passive subjunctive of κεύθω, ‘I am hidden’, and Ἄϊδι the dative ‘in Hades’. αὐτὸς ἐγών is ‘I myself’.

sentences.t:
τύμβον δ’ οὐ μάλα πολλὸν ἐγὼ πονέεσθαι ἄνωγα,
ἀλλ’ ἐπιεικέα τοῖον·
sentences.tr:
tymbon d’ ou mala pollon egō poneesthai anōga,
all’ epieikea toion·
sentences.l:
And a mound not very large I bid you labour at,
but a fitting one, of such a kind;
sentences.i: I do not bid you labour at a very large mound, but at one of fitting measure;
sentences.n: τύμβον is the mound heaped over a grave. οὐ μάλα πολλόν is ‘not very large’, with πολλός used of size. ἄνωγα is a perfect with present sense, ‘I bid’, taking the infinitive πονέεσθαι ‘to labour (at)’. ἀλλ’ ἐπιεικέα τοῖον is ‘but a fitting one, of such a kind’: a mound of suitable size, with τοῖον ‘such’ pointing to the measure he means. The unit ends in the middle of line 246.

sentences.t:
ἔπειτα δὲ καὶ τὸν Ἀχαιοὶ
εὐρύν θ’ ὑψηλόν τε τιθήμεναι,
sentences.tr:
epeita de kai ton Achaioi
euryn th’ hypsēlon te tithēmenai,
sentences.l:
and later, that one too, you Achaeans,
wide and high make it,
sentences.i: and afterwards, you Achaeans, make that mound, too, wide and high,
sentences.n: ἔπειτα δέ ‘and afterwards’. καὶ τὸν ‘that one also’ points back to the mound, τύμβον. Ἀχαιοί is addressed, and τιθήμεναι is the epic infinitive of τίθημι used as a command, ‘make it’. εὐρύν is the accusative of εὐρύς ‘wide’, and ὑψηλόν ‘high’. The unit begins in the middle of line 246.

sentences.t:
οἵ κεν ἐμεῖο
δεύτεροι ἐν νήεσσι πολυκλήϊσι λίπησθε.
sentences.tr:
hoi ken emeio
deuteroi en nēessi polyklēïsi lipēsthe.
sentences.l:
who after me
will be left among the many-thwarted ships.”
sentences.i: those of you who will be left behind me at the ships of many thwarts.”
sentences.n: οἵ κεν … λίπησθε is ‘you who shall be left’, with κεν and the subjunctive of λείπομαι (passive ‘be left behind’) making the relative clause general. ἐμεῖο is the epic genitive of ἐγώ, and δεύτεροι ‘second, after’ goes with it: after Achilles’ own death. πολυκλήϊσι ‘many-thwarted’ is the stock epithet of ships, κληΐς being the thwart or rowing-bench. Achilles’ speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἳ δ’ ἐπίθοντο ποδώκεϊ Πηλεΐωνι.
sentences.tr: hōs ephath’, hoi d’ epithonto podōkeï Pēleïōni.
sentences.l: So he spoke, and they obeyed the fleet-footed son of Peleus.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and they obeyed the fleet-footed son of Peleus.
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφαθ’ is the speech-closing formula ‘so he spoke’, ἔφαθ’ being ἔφατο, the middle past of φημί. ἐπίθοντο is the aorist middle of πείθομαι ‘obey’, taking the dative ποδώκεϊ Πηλεΐωνι: ποδώκης ‘fleet-footed’ and Πηλεΐων ‘son of Peleus’, both stock. The line begins a paragraph in the edition.

sentences.t:
πρῶτον μὲν κατὰ πυρκαϊὴν σβέσαν αἴθοπι οἴνῳ
ὅσσον ἐπὶ φλὸξ ἦλθε, βαθεῖα δὲ κάππεσε τέφρη·
sentences.tr:
prōton men kata pyrkaïēn sbesan aithopi oinōi
hosson epi phlox ēlthe, batheia de kappese tephrē·
sentences.l:
First with fire-faced wine they quenched the pyre throughout
as far as the flame had come, and the deep ash fell;
sentences.i: First they quenched the pyre with wine that has the look of fire, as far as the flame had come, and the deep ash settled;
sentences.n: The Greek of 237–238 is carried out almost word for word: κατὰ … σβέσαν is the aorist of σβέννυμι with tmesis, and σβέσαν the unaugmented aorist. ὅσσον ἐπὶ φλὸξ ἦλθε is ‘as far as the flame had come’, with ἐπί split from ἦλθε by tmesis. κάππεσε is κατέπεσε, ‘fell down’, and βαθεῖα τέφρη ‘deep ash’: the ash settles as the fire dies.

sentences.t:
κλαίοντες δ’ ἑτάροιο ἐνηέος ὀστέα λευκὰ
ἄλλεγον ἐς χρυσέην φιάλην καὶ δίπλακα δημόν,
sentences.tr:
klaiontes d’ hetaroio enēeos ostea leuka
allegon es chryseēn phialēn kai diplaka dēmon,
sentences.l:
and weeping, of their kindly companion the white bones
they gathered into a golden bowl and the double fat,
sentences.i: and, weeping, they gathered the white bones of their kindly companion into a golden bowl and the double layer of fat,
sentences.n: κλαίοντες ‘weeping’ is the present participle of κλαίω. ἑτάροιο ἐνηέος is the genitive of ἐνηής, ‘kindly’, which goes with ἑτάροιο ‘companion’. ἄλλεγον ‘were gathering up’ is the imperfect of a verb with a doubled λ built on λέγω ‘gather’, the verb of 239. ἐς … φιάλην and δίπλακα δημόν repeat Achilles’ words of 243.

sentences.t: ἐν κλισίῃσι δὲ θέντες ἑανῷ λιτὶ κάλυψαν·
sentences.tr: en klisiēisi de thentes heanōi liti kalypsan·
sentences.l: and having put it in the huts, with fine linen they covered it;
sentences.i: and put it in the huts and covered it with fine linen;
sentences.n: The object, the bowl with the bones, is not stated. θέντες is the aorist participle of τίθημι ‘put’, and ἐν κλισίῃσι ‘in the huts’, κλισίη being a hut or tent. ἑανῷ λιτί: λίς is a rare noun, here dative, for a linen cloth, and ἑανός ‘fine’ is of uncertain exact sense. The wording is that of the covering of the dead Patroclus at 18.352. κάλυψαν is the aorist of καλύπτω ‘cover’.

sentences.t:
τορνώσαντο δὲ σῆμα θεμείλιά τε προβάλοντο
ἀμφὶ πυρήν·
sentences.tr:
tornōsanto de sēma themeilia te probalonto
amphi pyrēn·
sentences.l:
and they marked out a tomb, and laid foundations
round about the pyre;
sentences.i: and they marked out the tomb and laid its foundations around the pyre;
sentences.n: τορνώσαντο is the aorist middle of τορνόω, ‘mark out by a line’ (from τόρνος, a tool for drawing a circle), here the ring the tomb will stand in. σῆμα is the ‘tomb’. θεμείλια ‘foundations’ is the neuter plural of θεμείλιον, and προβάλοντο the aorist middle of προβάλλω, ‘lay down before them’. ἀμφὶ πυρήν is ‘around the pyre’.

sentences.t:
εἶθαρ δὲ χυτὴν ἐπὶ γαῖαν ἔχευαν,
χεύαντες δὲ τὸ σῆμα πάλιν κίον.
sentences.tr:
eithar de chytēn epi gaian echeuan,
cheuantes de to sēma palin kion.
sentences.l:
and at once poured earth over it they poured,
and having poured up the tomb, back they went.
sentences.i: and at once they heaped the earth over it, and when they had heaped up the tomb they went back.
sentences.n: εἶθαρ is ‘at once’. χυτὴν γαῖαν is ‘earth that is poured, heaped’ (χυτός), and ἐπὶ … ἔχευαν is split by tmesis from ἐπιχέω. The aorist of χέω ‘pour’ is ἔχευα, and χεύαντες is the aorist participle. χέω is used for heaping a mound. πάλιν κίον ‘went back’ has κίον, the unaugmented imperfect of κίω. The unit begins in the middle of line 256 and ends at the full stop in 257.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Ἀχιλλεὺς
αὐτοῦ λαὸν ἔρυκε καὶ ἵζανεν εὐρὺν ἀγῶνα,
sentences.tr:
autar Achilleus
autou laon eryke kai hizanen euryn agōna,
sentences.l:
But Achilles
held the people back on the spot, and seated a wide gathering,
sentences.i: But Achilles held the people back where they stood and seated them in a wide gathering,
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ Ἀχιλλεύς turns to the next business. αὐτοῦ is the adverb ‘on the spot, right there’. ἔρυκε is the imperfect of ἐρύκω ‘hold back’, and ἵζανεν the imperfect of ἱζάνω ‘make sit’. ἀγών is the gathering, here the people sitting in a wide ring where the games will be run. The unit begins in the middle of line 257.

sentences.t:
νηῶν δ’ ἔκφερ’ ἄεθλα λέβητάς τε τρίποδάς τε
ἵππους θ’ ἡμιόνους τε βοῶν τ’ ἴφθιμα κάρηνα,
ἠδὲ γυναῖκας ἐϋζώνους πολιόν τε σίδηρον.
sentences.tr:
nēōn d’ ekpher’ aethla lebētas te tripodas te
hippous th’ hēmionous te boōn t’ iphthima karēna,
ēde gynaikas eÿzōnous polion te sidēron.
sentences.l:
and from the ships he brought out contest-prizes, cauldrons and tripods
and horses and mules and the mighty heads of oxen,
and well-girdled women, and grey iron.
sentences.i: and from the ships he brought out prizes, cauldrons and tripods, horses and mules and the mighty heads of cattle, and well-girdled women, and grey iron.
sentences.n: ἔκφερ’ is ἔκφερε, the unaugmented imperfect of ἐκφέρω ‘carry out’, and ἄεθλα are the prizes of a contest. The list runs through λέβητας ‘cauldrons’, τρίποδας ‘tripods’, horses and mules, and βοῶν ἴφθιμα κάρηνα ‘the mighty heads of oxen’, meaning cattle. ἐϋζώνους is ‘well-girdled’, and πολιὸν σίδηρον ‘grey iron’. Line 261 also stands at 9.365 and keeps the English it has there.

sentences.t:
ἱππεῦσιν μὲν πρῶτα ποδώκεσιν ἀγλά’ ἄεθλα
θῆκε γυναῖκα ἄγεσθαι ἀμύμονα ἔργα ἰδυῖαν
καὶ τρίποδ’ ὠτώεντα δυωκαιεικοσίμετρον
τῷ πρώτῳ·
sentences.tr:
hippeusin men prōta podōkesin agla’ aethla
thēke gynaika agesthai amymona erga iduian
kai tripod’ ōtōenta dyōkaieikosimetron
tōi prōtōi·
sentences.l:
For the horsemen, the fleet-footed ones, first splendid contest-prizes
he set out: a woman to lead away, knowing blameless works,
and an eared tripod of twenty-two measures,
for the first;
sentences.i: For the fleet-footed horsemen he first set out splendid prizes: a woman to take home, skilled in blameless crafts, and an eared tripod of twenty-two measures, for the winner;
sentences.n: The prizes for the chariot race, five of them, are set out in order; this first is for the winner. ἱππεῦσιν … ποδώκεσιν is ‘for the horsemen, the fleet-footed ones’, the stock epithet carried over to the riders. θῆκε is the aorist of τίθημι, ‘set out’. ἄγεσθαι is the middle infinitive ‘to lead away for oneself’. ἰδυῖαν is the perfect participle of οἶδα, ‘knowing’, here ‘skilled’. ὠτώεντα ‘eared’ means with handles, and δυωκαιεικοσίμετρον ‘of twenty-two measures’. The line begins a paragraph in the edition.

sentences.t:
ἀτὰρ αὖ τῷ δευτέρῳ ἵππον ἔθηκεν
ἑξέτε’ ἀδμήτην βρέφος ἡμίονον κυέουσαν·
sentences.tr:
atar au tōi deuterōi hippon ethēken
hexete’ admētēn brephos hēmionon kyeousan·
sentences.l:
and again for the second he set a mare
six years old, untamed, pregnant with a mule’s young;
sentences.i: and for the second he set a six-year-old mare, unbroken, with a mule’s young in her;
sentences.n: ἀτὰρ αὖ is ‘and again’, introducing the second prize. ἵππον here is feminine, ‘a mare’. ἑξέτε’ is the accusative ἑξέτεα of ἑξέτης ‘six years old’, with the final vowel elided, and ἀδμήτην means ‘untamed’, not yet broken to the yoke. βρέφος ἡμίονον is ‘a mule’s young’, the object of κυέουσαν, the present participle of κυέω ‘be pregnant with’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ τῷ τριτάτῳ ἄπυρον κατέθηκε λέβητα
καλὸν τέσσαρα μέτρα κεχανδότα λευκὸν ἔτ’ αὔτως·
sentences.tr:
autar tōi tritatōi apyron katethēke lebēta
kalon tessara metra kechandota leukon et’ autōs·
sentences.l:
and for the third he set an unfired cauldron
fine, holding four measures, still white just as it was;
sentences.i: and for the third he set a fine cauldron, unfired, holding four measures, still white just as it was;
sentences.n: τριτάτῳ is the epic form of τρίτῳ, ‘third’. ἄπυρον ‘unfired’ means not yet put over a fire, and λευκὸν ἔτ’ αὔτως ‘still white, just as it was’ says it has not yet been blackened by use. κατέθηκε is the aorist of κατατίθημι ‘set down’. κεχανδότα is the perfect participle of χανδάνω ‘hold, contain’; τέσσαρα μέτρα is ‘four measures’.

sentences.t: τῷ δὲ τετάρτῳ θῆκε δύω χρυσοῖο τάλαντα,
sentences.tr: tōi de tetartōi thēke dyō chrysoio talanta,
sentences.l: and for the fourth he set two talents of gold,
sentences.i: and for the fourth he set two talents of gold,
sentences.n: τετάρτῳ is ‘fourth’, and θῆκε ‘he set’ is the aorist of τίθημι. δύω is the epic form of δύο ‘two’, and χρυσοῖο the epic genitive of χρυσός ‘gold’. τάλαντα ‘talents’ are a weight; the Homeric talent was a small weight of gold, and its exact size is not known.

sentences.t: πέμπτῳ δ’ ἀμφίθετον φιάλην ἀπύρωτον ἔθηκε.
sentences.tr: pemptōi d’ amphitheton phialēn apyrōton ethēke.
sentences.l: and for the fifth a both-sides-set bowl, untouched by fire, he set.
sentences.i: and for the fifth he set a bowl of the ‘both-sides-set’ kind, untouched by fire.
sentences.n: ἀμφίθετον is of a meaning that is not known: the word is built from ἀμφί ‘on both sides’ and τίθημι ‘set’, and it may refer to handles or a fitting on each side. The English keeps its parts. ἀπύρωτον ‘untouched by fire’ is a different word from ἄπυρον of 267 and means the same thing, so it gets a different English. φιάλη is the shallow bowl.

sentences.t: στῆ δ’ ὀρθὸς καὶ μῦθον ἐν Ἀργείοισιν ἔειπεν·
sentences.tr: stē d’ orthos kai mython en Argeioisin eeipen·
sentences.l: and he stood upright and spoke a word among the Argives:
sentences.i: He stood up straight and spoke a word among the Argives:
sentences.n: στῆ is the aorist of ἵστημι, ‘stood’. ὀρθός ‘upright’ is the adjective, agreeing with the subject Achilles. μῦθον … ἔειπεν ‘spoke a word’ is a formula, and ἐν Ἀργείοισιν ‘among the Argives’ uses one of the poem’s names for the whole army. The colon introduces his second speech, which runs to the end of the part.

sentences.t:
Ἀτρεΐδη τε καὶ ἄλλοι ἐϋκνήμιδες Ἀχαιοὶ
ἱππῆας τάδ’ ἄεθλα δεδεγμένα κεῖτ’ ἐν ἀγῶνι.
sentences.tr:
Atreïdē te kai alloi eÿknēmides Achaioi
hippēas tad’ aethla dedegmena keit’ en agōni.
sentences.l:
“Atreus’-son and you other well-greaved Achaeans,
these contest-prizes lie awaiting the horsemen in the gathering.
sentences.i: “Son of Atreus and you other well-greaved Achaeans, these prizes are lying in the gathering, waiting for the horsemen.
sentences.n: Ἀτρεΐδη is the vocative ‘son of Atreus’, and ἐϋκνήμιδες Ἀχαιοί ‘well-greaved Achaeans’ is the stock address. ἱππῆας is the accusative plural of ἱππεύς ‘horseman’, and δεδεγμένα, the perfect participle of δέχομαι, here means ‘waiting for’. κεῖτ’ is κεῖται, a singular verb with the neuter plural ἄεθλα. ἐν ἀγῶνι is ‘in the gathering’, the place where the people sit.

sentences.t:
εἰ μὲν νῦν ἐπὶ ἄλλῳ ἀεθλεύοιμεν Ἀχαιοὶ
ἦ τ’ ἂν ἐγὼ τὰ πρῶτα λαβὼν κλισίην δὲ φεροίμην.
sentences.tr:
ei men nyn epi allōi aethleuoimen Achaioi
ē t’ an egō ta prōta labōn klisiēn de pheroimēn.
sentences.l:
If now we Achaeans were contending in contests for another man,
surely I, having taken the first prizes, would carry them to my hut.
sentences.i: If we Achaeans were holding these contests for some other man, I should surely take the first prizes and carry them off to my hut.
sentences.n: εἰ μέν with the optative ἀεθλεύοιμεν (ἀεθλεύω ‘contend in contests’) sets up a condition: ‘if we were contending’, and ἦ τ’ ἂν … φεροίμην, optative with ἄν, is the result, ‘I should carry off’. ἐπὶ ἄλλῳ is ‘for another man’, over another’s death. τὰ πρῶτα ‘the first prizes’. κλισίην δέ is ‘to my hut’, with the ending -δε of motion towards.

sentences.t: ἴστε γὰρ ὅσσον ἐμοὶ ἀρετῇ περιβάλλετον ἵπποι·
sentences.tr: iste gar hosson emoi aretēi periballeton hippoi·
sentences.l: For you know by how much in excellence my horses surpass:
sentences.i: For you know how far my horses surpass the others in excellence:
sentences.n: ἴστε is ‘you know’, the 2nd plural of οἶδα. ὅσσον is ‘by how much’. περιβάλλετον is a dual verb, ‘the two surpass’, with the plural ἵπποι: the pair of horses that draw Achilles’ chariot. The thing they surpass is not stated, so the English says ‘the others’. ἀρετῇ is a dative of respect, ‘in excellence’, and ἐμοί ‘mine’ goes with ἵπποι.

sentences.t:
ἀθάνατοί τε γάρ εἰσι, Ποσειδάων δὲ πόρ’ αὐτοὺς
πατρὶ ἐμῷ Πηλῆϊ, ὃ δ’ αὖτ’ ἐμοὶ ἐγγυάλιξεν.
sentences.tr:
athanatoi te gar eisi, Poseidaōn de por’ autous
patri emōi Pēlēï, ho d’ aut’ emoi engyalixen.
sentences.l:
for they are immortal, and Poseidon gave them
to my father Peleus, and he in turn put them into my hands.
sentences.i: for they are immortal, and Poseidon gave them to my father Peleus, who in turn put them into my hands.
sentences.n: ἀθάνατοι … εἰσι ‘they are immortal’. Ποσειδάων is the epic form of Ποσειδῶν, and πόρ’ is πόρε, the unaugmented aorist of πορεῖν ‘give’. πατρὶ ἐμῷ Πηλῆϊ ‘to my father Peleus’ is the dative of the receiver, the epic form of Πηλεῖ. ὃ δ’ αὖτ’ is ‘and he in turn’, Peleus, and ἐγγυάλιξεν is the aorist of ἐγγυαλίζω ‘put into the hands’.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἤτοι μὲν ἐγὼ μενέω καὶ μώνυχες ἵπποι·
sentences.tr: all’ ētoi men egō meneō kai mōnyches hippoi·
sentences.l: But indeed I shall remain, and the solid-hoofed horses;
sentences.i: But I shall stay where I am, and the solid-hoofed horses with me;
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἤτοι μέν is ‘but indeed’; the edition prints ἤτοι as one word. μενέω is the future of μένω, ‘I shall stay’ out of the race, and μώνυχες ἵπποι ‘the solid-hoofed horses’ is the stock phrase for horses with an undivided hoof, here in the nominative with a verb understood: ‘and (will stay) the horses’.

sentences.t:
τοίου γὰρ κλέος ἐσθλὸν ἀπώλεσαν ἡνιόχοιο
ἠπίου, ὅς σφωϊν μάλα πολλάκις ὑγρὸν ἔλαιον
χαιτάων κατέχευε λοέσσας ὕδατι λευκῷ.
sentences.tr:
toiou gar kleos esthlon apōlesan hēniochoio
ēpiou, hos sphōïn mala pollakis hygron elaion
chaitaōn katecheue loessas hydati leukōi.
sentences.i: for they have lost the good glory of such a charioteer, a gentle man, who very often poured liquid oil down on the manes of the two of them, after washing them with clear water.
sentences.n: γάρ gives the reason: the horses have lost their driver Patroclus, who is not named. τοίου … ἡνιόχοιο ‘of such a charioteer’ is the genitive going with κλέος ἐσθλόν, ‘good glory’. ἠπίου is ‘gentle’. σφωϊν is the dual dative ‘for the two’. ὑγρὸν ἔλαιον is ‘liquid oil’, and χαιτάων the epic genitive plural of χαίτη ‘mane’, with κατέχευε ‘poured down’. λοέσσας is the epic aorist participle of λούω ‘wash’, and λευκῷ ‘white’ here means clear.

sentences.t: τὸν τώ γ’ ἑσταότες πενθείετον,
sentences.tr: ton tō g’ hestaotes pentheieton,
sentences.l: Him the two, standing, mourn,
sentences.i: The two of them stand and mourn him,
sentences.n: τὸν is ‘him’, the driver of the previous unit. τώ is the dual article, ‘the two’, the horses. ἑσταότες is the epic perfect participle of ἵστημι ‘stand’ (Attic ἑστῶτες), and πενθείετον is the dual of the epic form of πενθέω, ‘mourn’. γε only stresses τώ.

sentences.t:
οὔδεϊ δέ σφι
χαῖται ἐρηρέδαται, τὼ δ’ ἕστατον ἀχνυμένω κῆρ.
sentences.tr:
oudeï de sphi
chaitai erēredatai, tō d’ hestaton achnymenō kēr.
sentences.l:
and to the ground for them
their manes are fixed, and the two stand grieving in heart.
sentences.i: and their manes are pressed to the ground, and the two stand grieving at heart.
sentences.n: οὔδεϊ is the dative of οὖδας ‘ground’, and σφι the epic dative ‘for them’, so ‘their’. χαῖται ‘manes’ is the subject of ἐρηρέδαται, the perfect passive of ἐρείδω ‘prop, press’, meaning the manes rest fixed on the ground as the heads hang. ἕστατον is the dual of the perfect of ἵστημι, ‘stand’, with present sense. ἀχνυμένω is the dual participle ‘grieving’, and κῆρ an accusative of respect, ‘in heart’. The unit begins in the middle of line 283.

sentences.t:
ἄλλοι δὲ στέλλεσθε κατὰ στρατόν, ὅς τις Ἀχαιῶν
ἵπποισίν τε πέποιθε καὶ ἅρμασι κολλητοῖσιν.
sentences.tr:
alloi de stellesthe kata straton, hos tis Achaiōn
hippoisin te pepoithe kai harmasi kollētoisin.
sentences.l:
But you others get yourselves ready throughout the army, whoever of the Achaeans
has trust in his horses and a well-joined chariot.”
sentences.i: But the rest of you, make ready throughout the army, whoever of the Achaeans trusts in his horses and his well-joined chariot.”
sentences.n: ἄλλοι is ‘the others’, the rest of the army, and στέλλεσθε, the imperative middle of στέλλω, means ‘get yourselves ready’, the sense being that those who want to race should prepare. ὅς τις Ἀχαιῶν is ‘whoever of the Achaeans’. πέποιθε is the perfect of πείθομαι with present sense, ‘trusts’, with the dative. ἅρμασι is plural for a single chariot, and κολλητοῖσιν ‘well-joined’ is ‘glued, fitted together’. Achilles’ speech ends here, and the next part begins with the formula that closes it.
